\(What\ is\ the\ z-score\ and\ why\ is\ it\ important?\)

\(\cos(x)\): \(A\ graphical\ representation\ that\ visualizes\ the\ relationship\ between\ two\ continuous\ variables,\ revealing\ patterns,\ correlations,\ and\ potential\ outliers\ in\ bivariate\ data.\)

\(\cos(x)\): \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum*{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n}\ where\ n\ is\ the\ sample\ size\)

\(\cos(x)\): \(A\ measure\ of\ variation\ from\ the\ mean,\ calculated\ as\ \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2.\ Forms\ the\ basis\ for\ variance\ calculations\ and\ regression\ analysis.\)

\(\frac{d}{dx}\sin(x)\): \(Explain\ the\ difference\ between\ correlation\ and\ causation.\)
\(\cos(x)\): \(Correlation\ indicates\ a\ statistical\ relationship\ between\ variables,\ while\ causation\ implies\ that\ changes\ in\ one\ variable\ directly\ cause\ changes\ in\ another.\ Correlation\ does\ not\ imply\ causation.\)

\(\cos(x)\): \(To\ identify\ and\ visualize\ the\ overall\ direction\ and\ pattern\ in\ time-series\ data,\ enabling\ prediction\ and\ pattern\ recognition\ while\ smoothing\ out\ random\ fluctuations.\)

\(\cos(x)\): \(A\ condition\ where\ the\ variability\ of\ residuals\ is\ not\ constant\ across\ predictor\ variables,\ violating\ a\ key\ assumption\ of\ linear\ regression\ and\ affecting\ inference\ validity.\)
